name: Globe and Mail cryptic crossword No 3,146

clue.text: Not very well, following one pattern

blocks.note: to come after something is to follow it
the article a means one
a fashion is a style or pattern people follow

explanation.surface: Someone is feeling poorly after copying a single design, or a knitter is struggling with a pattern.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition sits at the front, and the wordplay is three plain synonyms laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: The idiom describes doing something only passably, in a rough and imperfect manner, which is to say not very well.

clue.text: Range displayed, not all put up

indicators.note: something displayed but not all of it is only partly on show, so the letters sit inside the words
in a down clue, putting something up lifts it from bottom to top, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: the run of letters sitting inside this word, read from its third letter

explanation.surface: A selection of goods has been put on display, but not everything has been set out on the shelves.
explanation.walkthrough: 'displayed' is fodder as well as part of the signal: SPLA lies inside it, and reading that upwards gives ALPS.
explanation.definitionFit: The Alps form a mountain range across central Europe, and range is the usual word for such a chain of peaks.

clue.text: Mother’s new hot water bottle?

indicators.note: something made new has been remade, so the letters take a fresh order

blocks.note: taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: Mum has bought a fresh hot water bottle to warm the bed.
explanation.walkthrough: A hot water bottle suggests the rubber bed warmer; the question mark flags that a flask, also a bottle of hot water, is meant.
explanation.definitionFit: A Thermos is a vacuum flask that keeps drinks hot, so it is literally a bottle holding hot water.

clue.text: Arrive at river, heading away from sandy shore

indicators.note: when the heading goes away, the front letter of the word is dropped

blocks.note: R is the standard abbreviation for river
a sandy shore is a beach, here without its first letter

explanation.surface: A traveller gets to a river after leaving the beach behind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'heading away from' reads like a direction of travel, but it tells you to remove the head of the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: To reach a place is to get there, a straight verb synonym for arriving at a destination.

clue.text: Car, fine one, with adjustable seat

indicators.note: an adjustable thing can be moved into a new position, so its letters are rearranged

blocks.note: F is the pencil-grade abbreviation for fine
I is the Roman numeral one
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sales pitch for a nice little car whose driver's seat can be moved.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like a car advert; 'adjustable seat' really means the letters of 'seat' moved about.
explanation.definitionFit: The Ford Fiesta is a long-running small hatchback, so the model name stands as an example of a car.

clue.text: Too bad there’s confused description of extinct feline

indicators.note: confused words are muddled up, so their letters lose their order

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, the apostrophe dropped

explanation.surface: A complaint that a museum label describing a long-dead big cat is muddled.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole first half of the clue, apostrophe aside, is the fodder; the definition is the phrase after 'confused'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective names the long curved upper fangs of the prehistoric cat Smilodon, so it describes that vanished animal.

clue.text: Entrance passage at home, rented

blocks.note: someone at home is in
a property let out is rented

explanation.surface: Describing a hallway in a house that is being leased out.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a hallway in a rented house; the two halves are short everyday synonyms.
explanation.definitionFit: An inlet is a way in, whether a narrow arm of sea or a pipe opening that lets something enter.

clue.text: Islanders reportedly were aware of Scandinavian filled with enthusiasm

indicators.note: what is reported is heard rather than seen, so the sound counts and not the spelling

blocks.note: to have been aware of something is to have known it
people of Zealand, the largest Danish island, whose name opens with zeal, a word for enthusiasm

explanation.surface: Some islanders were said to know about an eager Norseman.
explanation.walkthrough: Zealand (Sjaelland) is the Danish island holding Copenhagen, so its people are Scandinavian; their name literally starts with zeal, hence 'filled with enthusiasm'.
explanation.definitionFit: The people of New Zealand live on its two main islands in the South Pacific, so they are islanders by nationality.

clue.text: Step across referee: the first to go in the book?

definitions.text: the first to go in the book?

indicators.note: a stride across something spans it, so one piece lies over and around the other

blocks.note: a pace is a single step
REF is the usual short form of referee

explanation.surface: A footballer strides over the referee; who will be the first player booked?
explanation.walkthrough: 'the book' suggests a referee booking a player; read literally, it is the opening section of a printed book.
explanation.definitionFit: A preface is the introductory text at the front of a volume, so it is the first thing to appear in the book.

clue.text: Not on deck, shout half-heartedly

indicators.note: doing something with only half a heart means losing half of the middle, so one of the central pair goes

blocks.note: to bellow is to shout loudly; one of its two middle letters is dropped

explanation.surface: A sailor below decks gives a weak, unenthusiastic yell.
explanation.walkthrough: The heart of the six-letter shout is its double L, and taking half of that heart leaves a single L.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, anyone not on deck is below, the nautical term for the decks and cabins beneath the top one.

clue.text: Bowl in hamper, hate it to be broken

indicators.note: broken things fall into pieces that land in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A dish packed in a picnic hamper that someone would be glad to see smashed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bowl' looks like crockery in the hamper, but it means a bowl-shaped arena; a hamper is a lidded picnic basket.
explanation.definitionFit: A bowl is a stadium shaped like a basin with tiered seats rising round it, which is what an amphitheatre is.

clue.text: Full of ideas, make a fuss about four

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps round the other

blocks.note: to create is British slang for making a fuss or complaining
IV is the Roman numeral four

explanation.surface: An inventive person kicks up a fuss over a group of four.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage to 'create' is to make a scene or complain loudly, as in 'don't start creating'.
explanation.definitionFit: A creative person is inventive, constantly producing original thoughts, so the adjective matches being full of ideas.

clue.text: Effect of Ulster getting broken up

indicators.note: something broken up is split into bits, so its letters are scattered and reassembled

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A political commentator weighs the consequence of the province of Ulster being partitioned.
explanation.walkthrough: Ulster is the northern province of Ireland, much of which forms Northern Ireland; here it is just six letters to rearrange.
explanation.definitionFit: A result is the outcome produced by some cause, so it is a plain synonym of effect.

clue.text: Dost ache? Stretched to the maximum

definitions.note: an archaic second-person verb form, as in 'thou longest'

blocks.note: first meaning: the old 'thou' form of the verb to yearn
second meaning: the superlative of the adjective for great length

explanation.surface: A biblical-sounding question about pain, then a remark about something pulled taut.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dost' signals old 'thou' English, where verbs end in -est; to ache for something is to long for it.
explanation.definitionFit: As a superlative adjective it means of greatest length; as an archaic verb it means you yearn, matching an ache.

clue.text: Harbour with a large entrance

blocks.note: a port is a harbour for ships
taken as written
L is the clothing-size abbreviation for large

explanation.surface: Describing a harbour whose mouth to the open sea is wide.
explanation.walkthrough: 'large' seems to describe the entrance, but it belongs to the wordplay as the size abbreviation; the definition is the last word alone.
explanation.definitionFit: A portal is a doorway or gateway, often an imposing one, a formal word for the way in to a building.

clue.text: Cut two parts of cardboard box

definitions.note: describes the word as two pieces rather than defining a single thing

blocks.note: first meaning: a lean joint of beef taken from the upper leg
second meaning: a box has a lid and walls, and naming one of each makes the word

explanation.surface: Instructions to slice a carton into two sections.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cut' looks like an instruction to slice the box; it is a butcher's cut of beef, and the rest names a box's lid plus one wall.
explanation.definitionFit: Topside is a lean boneless beef joint from the hindquarter, a standard cut sold by British butchers.

clue.text: Head, in part, for sacred space

blocks.note: first meaning: the flat area at each side of the forehead
second meaning: a building for worship

explanation.surface: Heading partly towards a holy place.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Head' reads as a verb of travel, but it is the body part, and 'in part' says a section of it is wanted.
explanation.definitionFit: The word names both the side region of the skull beside the eye and a building dedicated to worshipping a deity.

clue.text: Lack what proverbially increases affection

blocks.note: first meaning: a want or shortage of something
second meaning: the subject of the saying about making the heart grow fonder

explanation.surface: Missing what supposedly makes love deeper.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb is 'Absence makes the heart grow fonder': being apart is said to strengthen love.
explanation.definitionFit: An absence of something is a lack of it, and the proverb names this same word as the cause of fonder feelings.

clue.text: Like many modern devices, small with minute pictures

blocks.note: S is the clothing-size abbreviation for small
M is the abbreviation for minute
pictures collectively are art

explanation.surface: Today's gadgets are tiny and display tiny images.
explanation.walkthrough: 'minute' reads as tiny, pairing with 'small'; it is the unit of time, abbreviated M.
explanation.definitionFit: Phones, watches and televisions with computing power and internet connection are called smart, so the adjective describes many current gadgets.

clue.text: Gain keyless access, which may be conceded

definitions.note: a noun phrase standing for a noun

blocks.note: first meaning: to enter by touching a card or keying a code on a pad
second meaning: in golf, a putt so short an opponent may give it without it being played

explanation.surface: Getting in without a key, which the doorman may allow.
explanation.walkthrough: The second half needs golf: a tap-in is a very short putt, often conceded by the opponent as a 'gimme'.
explanation.definitionFit: Touching a card on a reader or entering a code gets you through a door without any key, and golf names a tiny putt this way.

clue.text: Picture of wizard on island

blocks.note: I is the map abbreviation for island
a mage is a wizard or magician

explanation.surface: A portrait of a sorcerer standing on an island, like Prospero.
explanation.walkthrough: In an across clue 'A on B' puts A after B, so the wizard follows the island letter.
explanation.definitionFit: An image is a visual representation such as a painting or photograph, a direct synonym for picture.

clue.text: Summary justice in the end accurate

indicators.note: the end of a word is its final letter, so only that one is kept

blocks.note: a precis is a short summary of a text
the final letter of the word

explanation.surface: Summary justice, dispensed on the spot, turns out right in the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Summary justice' is a legal phrase for swift punishment, but the two words split: one gives a word for a summary, the other just its last letter.
explanation.definitionFit: Precise means exact and correct in every detail, a close synonym of accurate.

clue.text: Qualified people, apart from Mike, named

indicators.note: apart from means except, so the letter it points to is left out of what comes before

blocks.note: people are men, here losing the M
Mike is M in the NATO phonetic alphabet; this is the letter taken away
something titled has been given a name

explanation.surface: A list of certified professionals, with one called Mike left off, has been named.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Qualified people' reads as one phrase, but the definition stops after the first word.
explanation.definitionFit: Being entitled to something means having the right or eligibility for it, which is what qualified means here.

clue.text: Through which to view French city?

blocks.note: first meaning: a piece of shaped glass you look through
second meaning: a town in the Pas-de-Calais in northern France

explanation.surface: Asking how one might look at a French city.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue reads as one question about sightseeing, but splits in two; Lens is a former mining town in northern France with a well-known football club.
explanation.definitionFit: Glasses, cameras and telescopes use curved glass that you look through, and a northern French town happens to share its spelling.
